title: What are readiness and liveness (and startup) probes, and what happens when each fails (readiness → removed from Service endpoints; liveness → container restarted)?
shortTitle: Readiness, Liveness, and Startup Probes in Kubernetes

s1_definition.profdef: Kubernetes probes are periodic health checks the kubelet runs against a container. A readiness probe decides whether a Pod should receive traffic — when it fails, the Pod is removed from the Service's Endpoints list but is NOT restarted. A liveness probe decides whether a container is still healthy — when it fails past its threshold, the kubelet restarts the container. A startup probe protects slow-starting apps by disabling the liveness and readiness checks until the application has finished booting.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India has a teller counter. The readiness probe is the "OPEN / CLOSED" sign on the counter — if the teller is on a tea break, the sign flips to CLOSED and customers are routed to other counters, but the teller is not fired. The liveness probe is the branch manager checking if the teller has fainted — if the teller does not respond at all, the manager replaces them. The startup probe is the grace period for a new teller still logging into the system in the morning — nobody judges them until they say "I am ready."
s1_definition.oneliner: Readiness controls traffic (remove from Service), liveness controls life (restart the container), and startup buys boot time for slow apps.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Kubernetes probes are periodic health checks the kubelet runs against a container. A readiness probe decides whether a Pod should receive traffic — when it fails, the Pod is removed from the Service's Endpoints list but is NOT restarted. A liveness probe decides whether a container is still healthy — when it fails past its threshold, the kubelet restarts the container. A startup probe protects slow-starting apps by disabling the liveness and readiness checks until the application has finished booting.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India has a teller counter. The readiness probe is the "OPEN / CLOSED" sign on the counter — if the teller is on a tea break, the sign flips to CLOSED and customers are routed to other counters, but the teller is not fired. The liveness probe is the branch manager checking if the teller has fainted — if the teller does not respond at all, the manager replaces them. The startup probe is the grace period for a new teller still logging into the system in the morning — nobody judges them until they say "I am ready."

**One line to remember:** Readiness controls traffic (remove from Service), liveness controls life (restart the container), and startup buys boot time for slow apps.

sections.s2_technical:
Each probe can use one of three mechanisms. An `httpGet` probe calls an HTTP endpoint and treats any 2xx or 3xx status as healthy, for example checking `GET /actuator/health/readiness` on port 8080. A `tcpSocket` probe checks whether a TCP port accepts a connection, useful for databases. An `exec` probe runs a command inside the container and treats exit code 0 as healthy, for example `exec: cat /tmp/healthy`.

Every probe has timing fields. `initialDelaySeconds` is how long to wait before the first check. `periodSeconds` is how often to repeat. `timeoutSeconds` is how long to wait for a response. `failureThreshold` is how many consecutive failures before acting, and `successThreshold` is how many consecutive successes before considering it healthy again, which must be 1 for liveness.

When a readiness probe fails, the kubelet reports the Pod as `NotReady`, and the EndpointSlice controller removes that Pod's IP from the Service. Traffic stops flowing to it immediately, but the container keeps running. This is correct for a banking service that is temporarily overloaded or waiting on a slow database connection pool — you do not want to kill it, you just want to stop sending it work until it recovers.

When a liveness probe fails past `failureThreshold`, the kubelet kills and restarts the container according to the Pod's `restartPolicy`. This is for unrecoverable states like a deadlocked thread pool. A senior nuance is that an aggressive liveness probe is dangerous: if the transfer service is slow because the database is slow, restarting it does not fix the database — it just causes a restart storm. So liveness should test "am I fundamentally alive," not "is my downstream healthy."

The startup probe solves a classic problem. A Spring Boot banking app with Flyway migrations might take 90 seconds to boot. If the liveness probe has a 10-second initial delay, it kills the app before it ever starts. The startup probe runs first; while it is still failing, liveness and readiness are suppressed. Once the startup probe succeeds once, the kubelet switches to the normal probes. You give the startup probe a generous `failureThreshold × periodSeconds` budget, for example 30 × 5 = 150 seconds, so slow boots are tolerated without loosening the steady-state liveness check.
sections.s3_banking:
At the National Bank of India we run a Transfer Service in Kubernetes. Three real problems pushed us to configure all three probes correctly.

Problem 1 — the service sometimes gets a burst of transfers and its HikariCP connection pool is temporarily exhausted. While it waits for connections it cannot serve new requests, but it is NOT broken. If Kubernetes kept sending it traffic, Rajesh's transfer would time out. This is exactly what a readiness probe fixes — when the pool is saturated, readiness returns down, the Pod is pulled out of the Service, traffic goes to healthy Pods, and when the pool recovers the Pod rejoins.

Problem 2 — occasionally a background thread deadlocks and the whole JVM stops processing anything. The process is still up but useless. This is exactly what a liveness probe fixes — a trivial liveness endpoint stops responding, Kubernetes restarts the container, and service is restored automatically.

Problem 3 — on cold start the service runs Flyway migrations and warms caches, taking about 80 seconds. Without protection the liveness probe would kill it mid-migration forever. This is exactly what a startup probe fixes — it tolerates the long boot, then hands over to liveness.

The mini-project is a runnable Java simulation of a `TransferHealthService` that models these three signals. It has an `Account` model with Rajesh and Priya, a connection-pool gauge, a liveness flag, and a startup flag. We will simulate the kubelet calling `checkStartup()`, `checkReadiness()`, and `checkLiveness()` over time and log how traffic and restarts are decided. We also show the real Kubernetes YAML for the three probes.

##### 4c. Configuration File

```yaml
# application.yml — Spring Boot Actuator health groups for probes
management:
  endpoint:
    health:
      probes:
        enabled: true          # exposes /actuator/health/liveness and /readiness
      group:
        readiness:
          include: db, redis, diskSpace   # readiness depends on downstreams
        liveness:
          include: livenessState          # liveness is a trivial "am I alive" check
  endpoints:
    web:
      exposure:
        include: health
```
sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Compile and run the probe simulation
javac -d out src/main/java/com/bank/transfer/*.java
java -cp out com.bank.transfer.ProbeSimulationDemo

# In the real cluster: watch readiness flip the Pod in/out of the Service
kubectl apply -f k8s/deployment.yaml
kubectl get endpoints transfer-service -w     # watch IPs add/remove on readiness changes
kubectl describe pod <pod> | grep -A3 Liveness # see restart count on liveness failures
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a Pod boots, serves a transfer, hits pool saturation, then deadlocks.

Step 1 — At t=0 the container starts. The kubelet calls the startup probe. Boot (Flyway migrations, cache warm) is not done, so `checkStartup()` returns false. During this time the kubelet does not run liveness or readiness, so the slow boot cannot trigger a restart.

Step 2 — At t=80 `finishStartup()` is called, boot completes, and the startup probe passes once. The kubelet now switches to normal liveness and readiness probing. Readiness returns true and the Pod's IP is added to the Service endpoints.

Step 3 — At t=85 a burst of transfers saturates the 2-connection pool. `checkReadiness()` sees `pool.isSaturated()` true and returns false. The EndpointSlice controller removes this Pod's IP from the Service. The container keeps running; no restart happens.

Step 4 — At t=90 a connection frees up, so Rajesh's transfer of fifty thousand rupees to Priya completes. Readiness returns true again and the Pod rejoins the Service endpoints.

Step 5 — At t=95 an internal deadlock sets the liveness flag down. `checkLiveness()` returns false; after the failure threshold the kubelet kills and restarts the container, which clears the deadlock.

Final output:

```
2026-10-30 00:50:01.100 [INFO] t=0  startup=false (kubelet suppresses liveness/readiness)
2026-10-30 00:50:01.105 [INFO] boot complete — migrations + cache warm done
2026-10-30 00:50:01.106 [INFO] t=80 readiness=true liveness=true
2026-10-30 00:50:01.107 [WARNING] READINESS DOWN: pool saturated 2/2 — pull from Service
2026-10-30 00:50:01.108 [INFO] t=85 readiness=false (removed from Service, NOT restarted)
2026-10-30 00:50:01.109 [INFO] t=90 transfer SAV2001->CUR3001 Rs.50000 done; readiness=true
2026-10-30 00:50:01.110 [SEVERE] LIVENESS DOWN: thread pool deadlocked — kubelet will restart container
2026-10-30 00:50:01.111 [INFO] t=95 liveness=false (kubelet restarts container)
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Pod starts (cold boot: Flyway + cache warm, ~80s)
    │
    ▼
  kubelet ── startupProbe ──→ /health/liveness
    │ started=false  → keep waiting, liveness/readiness SUPPRESSED
    │ started=true   → hand over to liveness + readiness
    ▼
  ┌──────────────── steady state ────────────────┐
  │                                               │
  │  readinessProbe /health/readiness             │
  │    pool OK   → Ready  → IP ADDED to Service    │
  │    pool FULL → NotReady → IP REMOVED (no kill) │
  │                                               │
  │  livenessProbe /health/liveness               │
  │    alive    → nothing                          │
  │    deadlock → RESTART container                │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  Transfer burst: SAV2001 → CUR3001 Rs.50000
    pool 0/2 → 2/2 (saturated) → readiness DOWN (traffic reroutes)
    pool 2/2 → 1/2 (freed)     → readiness UP   (rejoin Service)
    deadlock                   → liveness DOWN  → restart → recovered
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Kubernetes gives me three independent health probes, and the key to using them well is understanding that each one triggers a completely different action. A readiness probe answers whether a Pod should receive traffic right now, and when it fails the Pod is removed from the Service's endpoint list but is never restarted. A liveness probe answers whether a container is fundamentally alive, and when it fails past its threshold the kubelet kills and restarts the container. A startup probe answers whether a slow application has finished booting, and while it is still failing the kubelet suppresses the liveness and readiness probes so a long boot can never cause a restart loop.

The most important senior insight is to keep readiness and liveness semantically different. Readiness should reflect downstream health such as the database connection pool, because a saturated pool is a temporary condition where I want to stop sending traffic but keep the process alive. Liveness should be a trivial self-check that answers whether the process can serve anything at all, because if I wire a slow database into my liveness probe, a slow database triggers endless restarts that make the outage worse instead of better.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used exactly this split on our Transfer Service. The readiness group included the database and Redis, so when HikariCP was saturated during a burst of transfers the Pod was pulled out of the Service and traffic flowed to healthy Pods while the saturated Pod recovered on its own. The liveness probe was a bare liveness-state endpoint, so it only restarted the container on a true deadlock. And because our Spring Boot app ran Flyway migrations and cache warm-up for about eighty seconds, I gave the startup probe a generous budget of thirty failures at five-second intervals, which let the application boot cleanly without ever loosening the steady-state liveness threshold.

The practical payoff is resilience without flapping. Transient overload reroutes traffic instead of killing Pods, genuine hangs self-heal through restarts, and slow startups are tolerated, so Rajesh's transfer either succeeds on a healthy Pod or waits a moment for one to become ready, but it never lands on a dead or half-booted container.
